content: Directive 67/548/EEC, also known as the Council Directive of 27 June 1967, is the primary European Union legislation governing chemical safety. It establishes rules for the classification, packaging, and labeling of dangerous substances. This directive was enacted under Article 95 (formerly Article 100a) of the Treaty of Rome. It is also applicable in the European Economic Area (EEA) and ensures compliance with relevant Swiss laws. Scope of the Directive The directive applies to pure chemicals and chemical mixtures (referred to as preparations) that are placed on the market within the European Union. However, it does not apply to substances created solely for research purposes. Additional rules for chemical preparations are outlined in Directive 1999/45/EC. The directive explicitly excludes the following categories of substances and preparations: Medicines Cosmetics Waste Foodstuffs for humans or animals Pesticides Radioactive materials Furthermore, the directive does not apply to the transportation of dangerous substances or preparations. Classification of Dangerous Substances Article 2 of the directive defines the classes of substances or preparations considered dangerous. Some of these classes are associated with specific chemical hazard symbols and/or codes: Explosives (E) Oxidizing agents (O) Flammable substances or preparations, classified as extremely flammable (F+) or highly flammable (F) Toxic substances or preparations, classified as very toxic (T+) or toxic (T) Harmful substances or preparations (Xn) Corrosive substances or preparations (C) Irritants (Xi) Sensitizers Carcinogens (Carc.), categorized into three categories Mutagens (Mut.), categorized into three categories Substances or preparations toxic to reproduction (Repr.), categorized into three categories Substances or preparations dangerous to the environment (N) Substances or preparations falling into one or more of these classes are listed in Annex I of the directive, which is regularly updated. A public database of these substances is maintained by the European Chemicals Bureau. Danger Symbols The danger symbols associated with hazardous substances are defined in Annex II of the directive. A consolidated list of these symbols, including translations into other EU languages, is available in Directive 2001/59/EC. Standard Phrases Standard phrases are defined in Annexes III and IV of the directive. Annex III specifies phrases related to the nature of special risks associated with dangerous substances and preparations, commonly referred to as R-phrases. Annex IV defines phrases related to safety advice concerning dangerous substances and preparations, often referred to as S-phrases. These standard phrases must appear on the packaging and label of the product, as well as on its Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS). For substances listed in Annex I, the use of these standard phrases is mandatory. The lists of standard phrases were last updated in 2001, and Directive 2001/59/EC provides a consolidated list in all EU languages. Packaging Requirements (Article 22) The directive outlines specific requirements for the packaging of dangerous substances and preparations to ensure safety and compliance. Labeling Requirements (Articles 23-25) The label on the packaging of a dangerous substance or preparation must clearly display the following information: The name of the substance (for substances listed in Annex I, the name must match one of those listed in the annex; otherwise, the name should be internationally recognized). The name, full address, and telephone number of the person or company responsible for placing the substance on the market (manufacturer, importer, or distributor). The danger symbols, if applicable. The standard phrases, if applicable (certain exemptions are permitted). The EINECS number or equivalent. For substances listed in Annex I, the words EEC label. Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) Article 27 of the directive mandates that suppliers provide a Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) either in paper or electronic form at or before the first delivery of a dangerous substance or preparation. Suppliers are also required to inform users of any new relevant information that becomes available. Directive 2001/58/EC provides detailed guidance on the preparation of MSDS. Transposition into National Law A directive is binding on EU member states but cannot be enforced against individuals or companies until it has been transposed into the national law of the respective state. For example, in the UK, this directive was implemented through the Chemicals (Hazard Information and Packaging for Supply) Regulations 2002 (CHIP Regulations).
